title: Thin lenses — lens maker's formula and power of lens
topicTitle: Thin lenses — lens maker's formula and power of lens
notes: A thin convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays to a real focus. A concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges them. In the Cartesian convention a convex lens in air has positive f.

The lens-maker formula is 1/f = (μ − 1) (1/R1 − 1/R2). The signs of the radii follow the same convention: a surface whose centre is to the right of the surface has a positive radius when light travels to the right.
For a symmetric double-convex lens, R1 is positive and R2 is negative, so the two terms add. A higher index or a tighter curve means a shorter focal length.
The power is P = 1/f with f in metres. The unit is the dioptre. A lens of f = 0.25 m has power 4 D. Two thin lenses in contact have powers that add.
The thin-lens equation is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. A real object has negative u. A real image on the far side has positive v.
The formula assumes a thin lens and paraxial rays. A thick lens or a ray far from the axis needs a more careful treatment, and the simple power is then only a start.

keyPoints: A convex lens has positive power.

A shorter focal length is a stronger lens.
summary: The lens-maker formula builds 1/f from the index and the two radii. A symmetric convex lens of index 1.50 and radii 20 cm has f = 20 cm. Power is 1/f in metres, so that lens is 5.0 D. The imaging equation is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.
